severity_estimate: Moderate (Can lead to gingivitis and periodontitis if untreated)
possible_causes: Mineralization of unremoved dental plaque by calcium and phosphate in saliva
Inadequate oral hygiene practices (infrequent brushing or flossing)
High-sugar or high-carbohydrate diet
Chronic dry mouth (xerostomia)
Tobacco use and smoking
common_symptoms: Hardened, calcified yellow, brown, or black deposits near the gumline
Persistent bad breath (halitosis)
Red, swollen, or tender gums (gingivitis)
Bleeding gums during brushing or flossing
treatment_suggestions: Professional dental scaling and root planing performed by a dentist or dental hygienist
Ultrasonic scaling to shatter hard deposits
Professional tooth polishing to smooth enamel surfaces
Note: Hardened calculus cannot be removed by standard home brushing or flossing
prevention_tips: Brush teeth thoroughly twice daily for two minutes using fluoride toothpaste
Floss daily or use interdental brushes to remove plaque between teeth
Use a tartar-control toothpaste and alcohol-free antiseptic mouthwash
Schedule professional dental check-ups and cleanings every 6 months
Limit sugary snacks and beverage intake
when_to_see_a_doctor: Schedule a dental visit if you notice visible hardened yellow/brown crust near the gums, persistent gum bleeding, gum recession, or chronic bad breath.

severity_estimate: Moderate (Impacts mastication, speech, alignment, and facial aesthetics)
possible_causes: Genetic factors (mutations in genes such as MSX1, PAX9, or AXIN2)
Ectodermal dysplasia or other hereditary syndromes
Environmental disturbances during tooth organogenesis (e.g., maternal illness, radiation, severe pediatric infection)
common_symptoms: Congenital absence of 1 to 5 primary or permanent teeth (excluding third molars)
Abnormal gaps or wide spacing between existing teeth
Delayed eruption of adjacent permanent teeth
Difficulty in proper chewing or articulation of certain sounds
Over-retained primary (baby) teeth past normal shedding age
treatment_suggestions: Orthodontic therapy (braces or clear aligners) to align existing teeth or manage spacing
Dental implants (once facial growth is complete)
Fixed dental bridges or removable partial dentures
Pediatric dentistry monitoring and multidisciplinary care planning
prevention_tips: Hypodontia is a developmental/genetic condition; primary prevention is not possible
Early pediatric dental evaluation (by age 1 or upon tooth eruption) allows early space management
Genetic counseling for families with a history of missing teeth or ectodermal dysplasia
when_to_see_a_doctor: Consult a pediatric dentist or orthodontist if a child's primary teeth do not shed on schedule, if permanent teeth fail to erupt, or if noticeable gaps develop.

severity_estimate: Mild to Moderate (Self-limiting, usually resolves in 7–14 days)
possible_causes: Minor mechanical mouth trauma (accidental cheek biting, hard food, sharp dental work or braces)
Nutritional deficiencies (Vitamin B12, iron, folate, or zinc)
Emotional stress and systemic fatigue
Sensitivities to acidic, spicy, or citrus foods
Toothpastes containing Sodium Lauryl Sulfate (SLS)
Immune system reactivity or gastrointestinal conditions (e.g., Celiac, Crohn's disease)
common_symptoms: Small, round or oval lesions with a yellow/white center and inflamed red border
Pain or burning sensation localized inside the cheeks, lips, tongue, or soft palate
Localized swelling and heightened sensitivity while eating, drinking, or talking
treatment_suggestions: Topical OTC pain-relieving gels or pastes (e.g., containing benzocaine or triamcinolone)
Antimicrobial or steroid mouth rinses prescribed by a healthcare provider
Warm salt-water rinses to soothe inflamed tissues
Over-the-counter oral pain relievers (ibuprofen or acetaminophen) for discomfort
prevention_tips: Avoid trigger foods (excessively acidic, salty, or spicy items)
Switch to a soft-bristled toothbrush and use SLS-free toothpaste
Maintain a balanced diet rich in vitamins B12, iron, and zinc
Manage daily stress through relaxation techniques
when_to_see_a_doctor: Seek medical evaluation if ulcers persist beyond 2 weeks, are unusually large, spread continuously, cause severe unmanageable pain, or are accompanied by high fever or difficulty swallowing.

possible_causes: N/A - Standard healthy anatomical and physiological state without clinical pathology
common_symptoms: Clean, smooth enamel surfaces with no visible caries, calculus, or discoloration
Pink, firm, non-bleeding gum tissues fitting snuggly around teeth
Fresh breath and adequate, healthy salivary flow
Moist, smooth oral mucosa and tongue surface
treatment_suggestions: No restorative or curative treatment needed
Maintain existing preventive maintenance regimen
prevention_tips: Brush twice daily for 2 minutes with fluoride toothpaste
Floss or clean interdental spaces daily
Eat a nutrient-dense, low-sugar diet
Visit the dentist every 6–12 months for routine check-ups and prophylaxis
when_to_see_a_doctor: Continue regular preventive dental appointments every 6 to 12 months, or seek immediate attention if new symptoms (pain, bleeding, spots, or sensitivity) arise.

severity_estimate: Moderate to High (Progressive condition; can lead to pulp infection, abscess, or tooth loss)
possible_causes: Acid-producing bacterial biofilm (e.g., Streptococcus mutans) fermenting dietary carbohydrates
Frequent consumption of sugary, acidic, or sticky foods and beverages
Inadequate toothbrushing and lack of flossing
Insufficient exposure to topical fluoride
Dry mouth (reduced salivary flow and buffering capacity)
common_symptoms: Toothache, spontaneous pain, or localized throbbing
Tooth sensitivity to cold, hot, or sweet foods and drinks
Visible pits, dark spots, or holes in teeth
Pain when biting down or chewing
Brown, black, or chalky white staining on tooth surfaces
treatment_suggestions: Topical fluoride varnish/remineralization therapy (for early non-cavitated lesions)
Dental fillings (composite resin or dental amalgam) for cavity restoration
Dental crowns for extensive tooth structure loss
Root canal therapy if decay reaches the pulp/nerve tissue
Extraction if the tooth structure is unsalvageable
prevention_tips: Brush teeth twice daily with fluoridated toothpaste
Floss daily to remove plaque from proximal surfaces
Apply dental sealants on occlusal surfaces of molars (especially in children)
Limit frequency of sugar and refined starch consumption
Chew sugar-free xylitol gum to stimulate protective saliva production
when_to_see_a_doctor: Consult a dentist immediately if you experience tooth pain, sensitivity lasting past stimulus removal, visible dark spots or holes, or localized swelling around a tooth.

severity_estimate: Mild (Primarily cosmetic; can occasionally signal pulp necrosis or enamel erosion)
possible_causes: Extrinsic: Frequent consumption of dark foods/beverages (coffee, tea, red wine, cola, berries) and tobacco use
Extrinsic: Suboptimal plaque control and surface stain accumulation
Intrinsic: Fluorosis from excess fluoride ingestion during tooth development
Intrinsic: Childhood exposure to tetracycline antibiotics
Intrinsic: Dental trauma leading to pulp necrosis or internal hemorrhage
Age-related thinning of enamel exposing darker underlying dentin
common_symptoms: Yellow, brown, grey, or opaque white patches/stains on tooth surfaces
Loss of natural enamel translucency and shine
Uneven shade variations across single or multiple teeth
treatment_suggestions: Professional dental cleaning and stain polishing (extrinsic)
Professional in-office or custom take-home whitening/bleaching kits
Enamel microabrasion for superficial intrinsic spots
Composite bonding, porcelain veneers, or dental crowns for deep intrinsic staining or dead teeth
prevention_tips: Rinse mouth with water or brush after drinking dark beverages like coffee, tea, or red wine
Avoid smoking and chewing tobacco products
Maintain consistent daily oral hygiene (brushing and flossing)
Monitor fluoride intake in young children to prevent fluorosis
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a dentist if a single tooth turns gray/black (possible nerve death), if discoloration is accompanied by pain/chipping, or to get safe, professional whitening guidance.
